sourcesRead.title: Sam Kriss, "Why Does A.I. Write Like … That?" (print headline "The Omniwriter"), The New York Times Magazine
sourcesRead.route: live URL paywalled (43 bytes); Wayback capture 20260127025121id_ truncated at the paywall; full text from Wayback capture 20251221211413id_

claims.feature: other: sensory language attached to the immaterial
claims.claim: Sam Kriss argues that AI works sensory language into its prose but, lacking an anchor in the real world, attaches all of it to the immaterial.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: all of its sensory language ends up getting attached to the immaterial
claims.page: section after the Woolf 'plateful of blue water' passage
claims.routeHint: Wayback raw capture 20251221211413id_ of the NYT URL
claims.modelEra: ChatGPT-5 and Grok and Claude tested by the author in 2025; register measured: fiction, essays and corporate notices

claims.claim: Kriss reports that AI-generated fiction is obsessed with ghosts and that in machine-written fiction everything is spectral, a shadow, a memory or a whisper.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: In machine-written fiction, everything is spectral.
claims.page: section beginning 'But if you task an A.I. with the production of culture itself'
claims.modelEra: ChatGPT-5 era, tested 2025; register measured: fiction

claims.claim: Kriss reports that AI fiction describes things as quiet or softly humming for no obvious reason and often against the logic of the narrative.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: They also love quietness.
claims.modelEra: ChatGPT-5 tested 2025; register measured: fiction

claims.feature: other: measured tell count in one generated story
claims.claim: Kriss counted seven words in the roughly 1,100-word ChatGPT story Sam Altman presented as evidence of creative-writing ability: quiet, hum, humming, echo twice, liminal and ghosts.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: A.I.s are absolutely obsessed with ghosts
claims.page: same section, discussing Altman's metafictional short story
claims.modelEra: an early version of ChatGPT-5, 2025; register measured: fiction

claims.feature: other: reaching for the marker of a quality instead of the quality
claims.claim: Kriss's mechanism for the tells is that the model is constantly tickling the Simpsons: knowing good writing is subtle, it screams at the top of its voice that everything is subtle and quiet.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: it’s constantly tickling the Simpsons
claims.modelEra: ChatGPT-5 era; the Simpsons anecdote is from late 2022 ChatGPT; register measured: fiction and essays

claims.claim: Kriss names overfitting as the technical term for the pattern in which the model reproduces a marker correlated with a quality instead of the quality itself.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: The technical term for this is “overfitting,”
claims.modelEra: December 2025; register measured: general prose

claims.claim: Kriss's explanation for the em dash is that within training data it appears more often in texts marked as well-formed, high-quality prose.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: the em dash is more likely to appear in texts
claims.polarity: asserts (mechanism, offered as the simplest theory)
claims.confidence: medium — Kriss offers this as a hypothesis, noting even AI engineers are not certain how the products behave
claims.modelEra: December 2025; models unnamed for this point; register measured: public statements and prose

claims.claim: Kriss reports that telling a model directly to stop using em dashes typically produces an agreement that itself contains em dashes.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: But it’s strangely hard to get rid of them.
claims.confidence: medium — Kriss reports this from user complaints rather than his own logged trial
claims.modelEra: December 2025; models unnamed; register measured: chat responses

claims.claim: Kriss reports that asked for science fiction the model has an uncanny habit of naming the protagonist Elara Voss, with Kael the usual male name, and that hundreds of self-published Amazon books now use those names where before 2023 there were none.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: an uncanny habit of naming the protagonist Elara Voss
claims.page: section on overfitting and word choice
claims.modelEra: December 2025, models unnamed for the naming habit; register measured: fiction

claims.claim: Kriss reports that in PubMed abstracts the word delve appeared in roughly one in every 10,000 abstracts in 2022 and that by 2024 usage had shot up by 2,700 percent.
claims.source: Sam Kriss reporting published research, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: By 2024, usage had shot up by 2,700 percent.
claims.confidence: medium — a journalist's report of studies he does not name individually
claims.modelEra: 2022 to 2024, ChatGPT era; register measured: biomedical abstracts

claims.claim: Kriss asserts that AI is extremely fixated on the rule of threes and that in fiction it swaps the not-X-but-Y form for a more literary No X. No Y. Just Z.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: A.I. is also extremely fixated on the rule of threes.
claims.modelEra: December 2025; Bing 2023 example included; register measured: viral social posts and fiction

claims.claim: Kriss names as a tic that the model stops midway through a sentence to ask itself a question, more often in conversation than in generated essays.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: stopping midway through a sentence to ask itself a question
claims.modelEra: December 2025; register measured: chat and essays

claims.claim: Kriss argues that in the AI dismissive formula an X with Y and Z, one or both attributes are either already implicit in X or make no sense at all.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: either already implicit in X
claims.page: section on the 'an X with Y and Z' tic
claims.modelEra: ChatGPT, Grok and Claude each tested by the author, 2025; register measured: comic prose

claims.feature: other: too much consistency or none
claims.claim: Kriss argues the model cannot get the balance right: either it imposes too much consistency, making its language redundant, or too little, turning it into drivel.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: it imposes too much consistency, in which case its language is redundant
claims.page: section on the 'an X with Y and Z' tic
claims.modelEra: ChatGPT, Grok and Claude, 2025; register measured: comic prose

claims.claim: Kriss attributes the failure to the models never having experienced the world, so everything they know reaches them through statistical correlations within quantities of words.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: Everything they know about the world comes to them through statistical correlations
claims.page: section citing Woolf's 'great plateful of blue water'
claims.modelEra: December 2025; register measured: literary prose

claims.claim: Kriss cites a generated phrase describing a studio that smelled of turpentine and dreams as a cheap literary effect that AI cannot avoid, since all it can do is pile concepts until they collapse.
claims.source: Sam Kriss quoting his own ChatGPT-5 output, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: smelled of turpentine and dreams
claims.polarity: demonstration passage generated by the model and quoted to show the tell
claims.modelEra: ChatGPT-5, 2025; register measured: fiction

claims.claim: Kriss reports that researchers found most people vastly prefer AI-generated poetry to the actual works of Shakespeare, T.S. Eliot and Emily Dickinson.
claims.source: Sam Kriss relaying a study, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: most people vastly prefer A.I.-generated poetry to the actual works of Shakespeare
claims.confidence: medium — a journalist's summary of an unnamed study
claims.modelEra: December 2025; register measured: verse

claims.claim: Kriss characterises the resulting public voice as mixed metaphors and empty sincerity, impersonal and overwrought, and says it is how corporations and elected officials now speak.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: Mixed metaphors and empty sincerity. Impersonal and overwrought.
claims.page: section on the Starbucks closure notice
claims.modelEra: September 2025 Starbucks notice; register measured: corporate and civic notices

claims.claim: Kriss reports that British MPs began opening speeches with 'I rise to speak', an American convention, and that on a single day in June it happened 26 times.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: On a single day this June, it happened 26 times.
claims.modelEra: June 2025 Hansard; register measured: parliamentary speech

claims.claim: Kriss reports a Max Planck Institute for Human Development study that analysed more than 360,000 YouTube videos of extemporaneous academic talks and found AI language increasingly coming out of human mouths.
claims.source: Sam Kriss relaying a Max Planck study, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: analyzed more than 360,000 YouTube videos
claims.confidence: medium — a relay; the study itself was not fetched here
claims.modelEra: study described as recent as of December 2025; register measured: extemporaneous speech

claims.feature: other: what the machine says about itself is wrong
claims.claim: Kriss reports that ChatGPT describes its own prose as too clean and neutral, and asserts that this is not remotely true because the writing is not smooth or neutral but weird.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: It’s not smooth or neutral at all — it’s weird
claims.page: section beginning 'If we’re going to turn over essentially all communication'
claims.modelEra: December 2025, ChatGPT; register measured: general prose

claims.feature: other: parody passage in the AI voice
claims.claim: Kriss opens the essay with a paragraph written in the AI voice as a demonstration, whose clauses include the claim that the writing does not open up the tapestry of human experience.
claims.source: Sam Kriss, parody passage written by the author in the machine's voice, The New York Times Magazine, 2025
claims.quote: It doesn’t open up the tapestry of human experience
claims.polarity: parody/demonstration passage, not the author's own register
claims.modelEra: December 2025; register imitated: general essay prose
